subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.textbook_anchor: A Tour Around My Village — Students look at the picture of Chandan's village and describe what they see (p. 4)

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to imagine they are standing at the entrance of a village they have never visited. What would they look for first? A quick show of hands gathers two or three ideas, settling the class into an observational mood.

Students open Textbook p. 4 and spend an unhurried period studying the village scene in silence. Teacher prompts: notice every person, every building, every path. Students then write their description in their notebooks, naming what they see and where it is placed in the picture.

Pairs compare their written descriptions. Teacher asks: did your partner notice something you missed? Each pair adds at least one new detail to their own description. Teacher draws attention to how the well, the banyan tree, the post office, and the health centre sit in relation to each other.

Whole-class share: teacher collects one observation from each pair on the board under two columns — 'Places' and 'People'. Class reads the two lists together and notes that places and people appear side by side in every village.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe a community scene and record distinct places and people they notice in an organised way.
periods.section_context: Chandan's village picture; playground, post office, well, banyan tree, health centre, shopkeeper, school, police, road.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which place in the picture do you think the most people visit every day, and why?' This opens a conversation about how community elders traditionally gather under large shade trees — invite students to share whether they have seen something similar near their own home.

periods.textbook_anchor: A Tour Around My Village — Students explore their own locality and record in a table how the people and places they observe are connected to each other (p. 4)

time_bands.activity: Teacher begins with a brief mental walk: 'Close your eyes and picture the route you took to reach school this morning. What did you pass? Who did you see?' Students share aloud — two or three contributions build a shared picture of a real, local community.

Students open Textbook p. 4 and study the connection-table format shown there. They then draw a similar two-column table in their notebooks ('Person or Place' / 'Connected to…') and fill it using their own locality observations, writing at least four people-place connections they know from personal experience.

Small groups of three compare tables. Each group picks the connection they found most surprising — one they had not thought about before — and prepares to share it with the class. Teacher circulates, listening for connections that span the natural and human worlds (e.g., the well connected to the farmer connected to the crop).

Groups share their 'most surprising connection'. Teacher notes these on the board and closes by asking: if one of these people or places were missing, how would the others be affected? Students respond briefly in their notebooks — one sentence.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and articulate how people and places in a community depend on one another.
periods.section_context: Students' own locality; people-and-place connections table; community interdependence.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt the group sharing with: 'Is the person or place you chose something that exists in every locality in India, or only in some places?' This helps students notice regional variety in community structures without the teacher prescribing a single answer.

periods.activity_title: Why Shared Places Matter — Van Mahotsav Poster
periods.section_ref: Van Mahotsav: A Festival for Planting Trees
periods.textbook_anchor: Van Mahotsav: A Festival for Planting Trees — Students create a colourful poster to invite people from their neighbourhood to participate in Van Mahotsav (p. 6)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the opening of the Van Mahotsav section from Textbook p. 5 and pauses at the three discuss prompts: why shared places matter, what life would be like without them, and how to keep them clean. Students respond briefly in a whole-class oral exchange — no writing yet. The aim is to anchor students emotionally in the value of shared spaces before the making task.

Teacher explains the poster task from Textbook p. 6: the poster must invite neighbours to join Van Mahotsav and communicate why it matters. Students decide individually: which shared place in their own locality are they celebrating? They note their chosen place and one reason it matters at the top of their paper before drawing begins.

Students design and colour their invitation poster. The poster must include: the name of the festival (Van Mahotsav), the shared place being celebrated or planted near, a visual that shows people coming together, and at least one line of welcoming text. Teacher circulates, encouraging students to represent the specific people — young, old, from different occupations — who would attend.

Gallery walk: posters are placed on desks and students do a quick look round the classroom. Teacher invites two volunteers to read their welcoming text aloud and explain why they chose their particular shared place.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express the value of shared community spaces through a visual and written creative product.
periods.section_context: Van Mahotsav festival (1–7 July, rainy season); shared public places — parks, schools, hospitals, bus stops; invitation poster for community participation.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: As students design their poster, ask: 'What would happen to this place if nobody looked after it for a whole year?' This draws out the connection between community care and the health of shared spaces, which is at the heart of the festival's purpose.

periods.textbook_anchor: Helping Hands in the Community — Students identify people who help maintain their locality and record their occupations (p. 7)

time_bands.activity: Teacher describes the banyan-tree scene from the chapter: parents and community members gathering to plan Van Mahotsav, each bringing a different skill. Students listen, then open Textbook p. 7 and look at the illustration. Teacher asks: can you spot at least three different kinds of workers in this picture?

Students draw a two-column table in their notebooks — 'Community Helper' and 'What They Do / Why It Matters' — and fill it with people who maintain their own locality. They aim for at least five distinct helpers, drawing from the textbook scene and from their own neighbourhood. Teacher notes: think about people you see every week — not just the most obvious ones.

Pairs compare lists. For each helper one partner listed that the other did not, they must agree on what that person does and add them to their own table. Teacher circulates and prompts: is there anyone who takes care of the roads, the lights, the water supply, the trees? Are there helpers whose work is less visible?

Class pool: teacher draws a quick web on the board with 'Our Locality' at the centre. Students call out helpers; teacher writes each on a spoke with a one-word descriptor of their role. Students copy the web and add any helpers from their own list that were not called out.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and record the different roles community members play in maintaining shared local spaces.
periods.section_context: Banyan-tree community gathering; carpenter, electrician, plant nursery owner (Noor), mason; community helpers and their occupations in students' own localities.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'The carpenter fixes benches, the electrician fixes the street light — both are working for everyone, not just themselves. Can you think of any work in your community that is done for everyone, not for money?' This surfaces the idea of voluntary or collective labour, which runs through the chapter's cultural strand.

periods.activity_title: Tools, Materials, and Skills for the Park
periods.textbook_anchor: Helping Hands in the Community — Students list different kinds of work required for developing and maintaining a park, with the materials, tools, and skills involved (p. 8)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook park-maintenance table with mason example (p. 8)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the mason example from the park-maintenance table on Textbook p. 8 aloud: what the mason does, the materials used (cement, bricks), the tools (trowel, level), and the skill required. Students follow in their textbooks. Teacher asks: what other kinds of work does a park need besides building walls?

Students open Textbook p. 8 and copy the table format into their notebooks, then fill at least four additional rows beyond the mason example. For each type of work, they write: the kind of work, the materials needed, the tools used, and the skill the worker must have. Students work individually in silence for this unhurried inquiry task.

Groups of three compare tables. Each group agrees on which row they found hardest to fill and discusses why — was it because the work is rarely seen, or because the materials are hard to name? One member of each group prepares to share their group's hardest row with the class.

Groups share their hardest rows. Teacher adds them to a class table on the board. Students copy any rows they had missed. Teacher closes: every kind of work in the table requires a real skill — no occupation in the list is more or less important than the others.

periods.implied_lo: Students can systematically analyse a community maintenance task by identifying the work type, materials, tools, and skills involved.
periods.section_context: Park development and maintenance; mason (cement, bricks, trowel), and additional park workers; materials, tools, skills table.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: As students fill the table, ask: 'Is any of the work in your table something that only men do, or only women do? What do you think about that?' This opens a dialogue about the equitable distribution of community labour without the teacher prescribing an answer.

periods.activity_title: Community Solidarity — The Bridge Story and Local Memory
periods.textbook_anchor: Celebrating Van Mahotsav — Students discuss whether it is important for communities to come together in times of need (p. 10)

time_bands.activity: Teacher narrates the Kanker, Chhattisgarh story from the chapter: a flooded river, the Chinar; the entire community working together to build a bamboo-and-stone bridge in two days so that students and villagers could cross safely. Students follow in Textbook p. 10. Teacher pauses after the narration: what made this possible?

Class discussion using the two discuss prompts on Textbook p. 10: why is it important for communities to come together in times of need, and do people in your own locality support each other in this way? Teacher facilitates without driving toward a single conclusion — every student's local example is valid. Students are invited to share one remembered occasion.

Students write independently in their notebooks: a short account (three to five sentences) of one occasion — real or imagined — when people in their locality came together to solve a shared problem. They describe who was involved, what the problem was, and how cooperation helped.

Three or four volunteers share their accounts aloud. Teacher points out: did anyone's story involve a natural event — rain, flood, drought, a fallen tree? Did anyone's story involve a celebration or a festival? The class notices that communities gather for both difficulties and celebrations.

periods.implied_lo: Students can recall and articulate examples of community cooperation and explain why collective action matters in a shared locality.
periods.section_context: Van Mahotsav celebration — cleaning, planting, watering, cooking groups; Kanker, Chhattisgarh bamboo-and-stone bridge over Chinar river (2024); community solidarity discussion.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'The bridge in the story was built from bamboo and stone — materials found nearby. Why do you think the community used those particular materials instead of buying others?' This surfaces traditional knowledge of locally available resources without labelling it as such.

periods.activity_title: The Shared Feast — Food, Leaves, and Festival Traditions
periods.textbook_anchor: Sharing a Meal — Students write about how their family or community works together while preparing for a festival or other occasion (p. 11)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook shared-feast and Bhela Ghar illustration (p. 11)

time_bands.activity: Teacher describes the chapter's post-plantation feast scene: vegetables and cereals contributed by different villagers, served on banana leaves, with the leaves later placed in a pit to make manure. Students open Textbook p. 11 and locate the illustration. Teacher asks: why do you think banana leaves were used instead of plates? What happens to the leaves at the end?

Teacher introduces Uruka — the first day of Magh Bihu on 14 January in Assam — and the Bhela Ghar, a bamboo-and-hay hut built and then ritually burnt as part of the celebration, followed by a communal feast. Class discusses: what do the village feast in the chapter and Uruka have in common? What is different? Students speak from their seats; teacher maps similarities and differences on the board.

Students write independently in response to the Textbook p. 11 prompt: how does their family or community work together when preparing for a festival or a special occasion? They describe at least two specific tasks that different people take on, and note whether any materials used come from nature.

Volunteers share their written responses. Teacher collects on the board: what natural materials were mentioned (leaves, flowers, clay, bamboo, hay)? Students notice that community feasts and festivals across different regions share the feature of people contributing different things to make one shared experience.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe how families and communities distribute roles and use natural materials collectively during festivals and shared meals.
periods.section_context: Post-plantation feast; banana leaves as plates and composting in a pit; Uruka (first day of Magh Bihu, 14 January, Assam); Bhela Ghar (bamboo-and-hay hut); communal feast traditions.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'In the chapter, banana leaves are placed in a pit after eating — what do you think that teaches us about how people thought about waste before there were dustbins?' This draws out the composting practice as inherited environmental wisdom without naming the tradition as a category.

periods.activity_title: Our School, Our Team — Role Mapping and Reflection
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students write the different roles people play in their school (teachers, students, caretakers, bus drivers, etc.) (p. 13)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with the two discussion prompts from Textbook p. 13: how can we take care of nature and our neighbourhood, and how does helping others and working together make our community better? Students respond briefly in a whole-class exchange. Teacher does not lecture; the goal is to hear students' own language for these ideas.

Students write individually in their notebooks, responding to the Textbook p. 13 reflection prompt: they list the different roles people play in their school community — teachers, students, caretakers, bus drivers — and for each role, they write one sentence explaining how that role helps the whole school function. They aim for at least five distinct roles.

Students form small groups of four or five and share their role lists. The group agrees on one role that is often overlooked and discusses: what would change in the school if this role disappeared? Each group nominates a spokesperson to share the group's chosen role and reasoning.

Groups share their chosen overlooked role. Teacher closes: every person in this school — seen or unseen — makes it possible for learning to happen. Students add to their written list any role they had not thought of before.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify the roles different members play in a shared institution and explain how each role contributes to the whole community's functioning.
periods.section_context: School community roles — teachers, students, caretakers, bus drivers; 'Our School, Our Team!' reflection; community care and helping norms.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there anyone in this school whose work happens before you arrive or after you leave — someone you might never see? What do they do?' This surfaces invisible labour and encourages students to widen their circle of recognition.

periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students choose a public place and create a riddle about it for friends to solve (p. 16)
materials: Optional: crayons for illustrating the riddle

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 15 and work through the riddle-matching activity — matching each riddle to its picture-solution. Teacher gives students time to attempt all riddles individually before discussing answers as a class. The class confirms which public place each riddle described.

Teacher directs students to Textbook p. 16: now they will create their own riddle about a public place of their choice. Teacher models briefly on the board: choose a place, think of three clues that describe it without naming it, and write the clues as questions or statements. Students decide which place they will riddle about.

Students compose their own riddles in their notebooks. The riddle must have at least three clues, must not name the place directly, and may optionally include a small illustration. Teacher circulates, checking that clues are specific enough to point to one answer but not so obvious that the first clue gives it away.

Pairs exchange notebooks and try to solve each other's riddle. Partners give feedback: was the riddle too easy, too hard, or just right? Students make one revision to their riddle based on their partner's response. Two or three volunteers read their riddles aloud for the whole class to solve.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent the characteristics of a community place through a structured creative format and evaluate whether their representation communicates clearly.
periods.section_context: Textbook riddle-matching activity (p. 15); public places — community riddle solutions; student-created riddle about a chosen public place (p. 16).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If a friend from a completely different region of India tried to solve your riddle, would they get it? Or does your riddle only work for people who already know your locality?' This nudges students to think about what is universal and what is local about the places they chose.

periods.activity_title: Living Together — Bringing the Chapter Together
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students create three groups, each identifying a situation in their locality that needs improvement and planning activities to address it (p. 16)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a brief oral synthesis: this chapter has moved from observing a village scene to understanding that every community — whether a village, a town, or a school — depends on shared spaces, shared work, and shared celebration. Teacher asks: what is one idea from the chapter that surprised you or changed the way you see your own neighbourhood?

Students form three groups as directed on Textbook p. 16. Each group identifies a real situation in their locality that needs improvement — related to cleaning, helping others, or organising an event — and completes the planning table: what is the situation, who is affected, what activities would help, and who would need to be involved. The Khetala model from Sikkim — agricultural specialists who come together at harvest time to support one another — serves as an example of how communities organise cooperative effort around a shared need.

Each group shares their chosen situation and proposed activities with the class. Class members ask one question to each presenting group. Teacher connects each group's proposal back to themes from across the chapter: community interdependence, the value of shared spaces, the roles of different helpers, and the traditions that bind communities together — from Van Mahotsav to Magh Bihu's Uruka feast, from banana-leaf composting to bamboo bridge-building.

Students write individually in their notebooks: one sentence describing a community tradition or practice — from the chapter or from their own family — that shows how people and nature are connected; and one sentence describing a role they themselves could play in keeping their locality healthy and welcoming. Notebooks close and teacher invites two or three final shares.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect community roles, shared spaces, cultural practices, and cooperative action into a coherent understanding of how people live and work together.
periods.section_context: Group situation-improvement planning table (p. 16); Khetala agricultural cooperation (Sikkim); synthesis of chapter themes — community interdependence, Van Mahotsav, Magh Bihu/Uruka, Bhela Ghar, banana-leaf composting, bamboo bridge (Kanker), school roles, shared spaces.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: As groups share, ask: 'The Khetala specialists in Sikkim each bring a different skill to harvest time — just like the carpenter, the electrician, and the nursery owner in the chapter. Can you see that same pattern in your own group's plan?' This helps students recognise that the chapter's core idea — different people, different skills, one shared goal — applies across very different cultural and geographic settings.

assessment_items.question_text: Chandan's village has a well, a banyan tree, a post office, a health centre, and a playground. Which of the following best describes what these places have in common?

options.label: A
options.text: They are all built by the government alone and not used by villagers.

options.label: B
options.text: They are all found only in villages and never in towns or cities.

options.label: C
options.text: They are places that only children are allowed to visit.

options.label: D
options.text: They are shared spaces that different people in the community use and depend on.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. This item checks whether the student has moved from listing individual places to understanding what makes them community spaces — the core concept of the opening section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe a community scene and record distinct places and people they notice in an organised way.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not understood the idea of shared community ownership and has attributed these spaces entirely to a single external authority — a misconception about how local institutions function.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has narrowed their reading to the child characters in the chapter (Chandan's perspective) and missed the broader community use described in the scene.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has over-generalised from the village setting and confused the specific context of the chapter with a universal claim, missing that the concept of shared spaces applies beyond villages.

assessment_items.question_text:
A student made the following table about their locality. One row is done for you as an example:

| Person or Place | Connected to… |
|---|---|
| The well | The families who fetch water every morning |

Add two more rows to show how different people or places in a community are connected to each other.
expected_elements: At least two additional rows in the table, each with a named person or place from the student's own locality.
Each connection must show a clear dependency or relationship (not merely that the two things exist near each other).
At least one connection should involve a service or function (e.g., a health worker connected to sick community members, a road connected to people who travel to the market).
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any locally valid people-place connections. Answers will vary by region and locality — mark on the clarity of the described relationship, not on which specific places or people are named. A student who writes only names without explaining the connection has not met the expected element.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and articulate how people and places in a community depend on one another.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

assessment_items.task: You are helping to invite people to Van Mahotsav in your locality. Design a poster that tells neighbours why a specific shared place (a park, a school ground, a garden, or any other public space you know) is important and invites them to come and help plant trees or clean the space together.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My poster is about: ___________
One reason this place matters to our community: ___________
What I want people to come and do: ___________
A welcoming message (one or two sentences): ___________
[Draw your poster in the space below — include at least one picture and your written message.]
format_of_output: A drawn and written poster on plain paper or in the notebook, showing a named shared place, a reason it matters, an activity invitation, and a welcoming message.
assessment_items.annotation: This is a creative product task. Mark on whether the student has named a real shared place, expressed why it matters (not just that it is 'good' or 'nice'), and included an invitation that communicates the spirit of collective care. The visual need not be artistically accomplished — assess the clarity of the message.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Van Mahotsav: A Festival for Planting Trees
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express the value of shared community spaces through a visual and written creative product.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can articulate the civic value of a shared natural or public space and communicate it persuasively to others — moving from personal observation to collective call-to-action.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold walks the student through: identifying the place, giving one substantive reason it matters, naming a concrete action, and composing a welcoming message. A student who completes all four scaffold steps and adds a drawing has met the full task.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names a specific place, gives a reason tied to community use or nature (e.g., 'this park gives us shade and clean air'), and writes an invitation that mentions a specific action (planting, cleaning). Weak: writes only 'our park is nice' and draws a generic tree without connecting the poster to community participation.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot draw may use labels and arrows to show what their poster depicts. Students from localities without a formal park may use any shared open space — a school ground, a roadside tree, a common courtyard. All regional choices are valid.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The poster format mirrors the chapter's own task (Textbook p. 6) and directly demonstrates the competency of expressing conservation and sharing of natural resources in a communicative, public-facing mode.

assessment_items.question_text: In the chapter, a carpenter fixes benches, an electrician repairs the street light, and a nursery owner brings saplings — all for the same park. What does this show about community maintenance?

options.label: A
options.text: Different people contribute different skills to keep a shared space working for everyone.

options.label: B
options.text: Maintaining a public place is the responsibility of children, not adults.

options.label: C
options.text: One very skilled person can do all the work needed for a public place.

options.label: D
options.text: Only people with official jobs can help maintain a public place.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is C. This item tests whether the student has understood the division-of-labour theme at the heart of the section — that community spaces are maintained through diverse, complementary contributions.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and record the different roles community members play in maintaining shared local spaces.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has conflated 'community helper' with 'official employee' and missed the chapter's emphasis on informal community members contributing their personal skills.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has not read the diversity of workers in the scene and has defaulted to a single-expert model — a confusion between individual expertise and collective effort.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has over-identified with the child characters in the story and misread the adult-community-gathering scene, reversing the adult-child responsibility relationship described.

assessment_items.question_text:
Look at the table started below. The mason's row is completed as an example. Fill in one more row for a different worker needed to maintain or improve a park.

| Type of work | Materials needed | Tools used | Skill required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Building a wall | Cement, bricks | Trowel, spirit level | Knowing how to measure and lay bricks evenly |
| ___________ | ___________ | ___________ | ___________ |
expected_elements: A named type of work that is genuinely needed for park upkeep (e.g., planting, painting, watering, electrical repair, gardening).
At least one plausible material for that type of work.
At least one named tool appropriate to that type of work.
A brief description of the skill the worker needs — not just the job title.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any park maintenance occupation the student can meaningfully describe. Do not penalise unfamiliar occupations if the materials, tools, and skill described are internally consistent. A response that names a job title but leaves materials and tools blank has not met the full expected elements.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can systematically analyse a community maintenance task by identifying the work type, materials, tools, and skills involved.

assessment_items.question_text: In 2024, the people of Kanker in Chhattisgarh built a bamboo-and-stone bridge over the Chinar river in just two days when the river was flooded. Do you think communities should wait for the government to solve such problems, or should they act together on their own? Give reasons for your answer using what you have read and what you know from your own experience.
look_for: A clear position taken by the student (not just a description of the event).
At least one reason drawn from the chapter — e.g., the speed of the community response, the use of locally available materials, the fact that it enabled students to reach school safely.
At least one reason or example drawn from the student's own locality or general experience.
Recognition that both government and community action can play a role — a nuanced response is stronger than an absolute one-sided answer.
An argument that goes beyond 'it is good to help others' to explain why community cooperation specifically matters in emergencies or shared challenges.
assessment_items.annotation: This is an evaluative response item. Do not impose a single correct answer — both 'communities should act' and 'government and community should work together' are acceptable positions if well-reasoned. Award marks for the quality of reasoning and use of evidence, not for arriving at a particular conclusion.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can recall and articulate examples of community cooperation and explain why collective action matters in a shared locality.

assessment_items.question_text: After the Van Mahotsav tree plantation, the community in the chapter ate a feast together. The banana leaves used as plates were placed in a pit to make manure. In Assam, during Uruka (the first day of Magh Bihu), communities build a bamboo-and-hay structure called Bhela Ghar and share a communal feast. What do these two practices have in common? Write two things.
expected_elements: Identification that both practices involve communities coming together to share food collectively.
Identification that both practices use natural materials (banana leaves / bamboo and hay) rather than manufactured ones.
Optionally: recognition that both practices connect a cultural celebration or community event to the natural environment — scoring this as an additional strength if present.
assessment_items.annotation: The item requires two similarities. Award one mark per valid similarity up to two. A response that describes only one practice without comparing it to the other has not met the item's demand. Students are not expected to know details of Magh Bihu beyond what the chapter describes.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how families and communities distribute roles and use natural materials collectively during festivals and shared meals.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: Identification that both practices involve communities coming together to share food collectively.
Identification that both practices use natural materials (banana leaves / bamboo and hay) rather than manufactured ones.
Optionally: recognition that both practices connect a cultural celebration or community event to the natural environment — scoring this as an additional strength if present.

assessment_items.task: Think about your school as a community — just like the village in the chapter. Write about the different roles that people in your school play, and explain how each role helps the whole school work well. Then choose one role you think is often overlooked and explain why it matters.
assessment_items.scaffold:
People in my school and their roles:
1. ___________ — they help by ___________
2. ___________ — they help by ___________
3. ___________ — they help by ___________
4. ___________ — they help by ___________

The role I think is often overlooked: ___________
Why this role matters to the whole school: ___________
format_of_output: Written response in the notebook following the scaffold, with at least four roles listed and one 'overlooked role' explanation of at least two sentences.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any school roles the student names — there is no fixed list. Assess on: whether the student explains the function of each role (not just names the job title), and whether the 'overlooked role' explanation goes beyond 'they work hard' to say what would be missing or worse if that role did not exist.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify the roles different members play in a shared institution and explain how each role contributes to the whole community's functioning.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can transfer the chapter's community-interdependence concept to their own immediate institutional context (the school) and articulate why diverse, less-visible roles matter — demonstrating analytical thinking about community functioning.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold asks for four roles (with functions) and one 'overlooked role' explanation. A complete response fills all scaffold lines with genuine functional descriptions, not just job titles.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names a less obvious role (e.g., the person who cleans the classrooms, the cook, the gardener) and explains specifically what would go wrong without it. Weak: lists only teachers and students, describes roles as 'they do their job well', and gives an overlooked role explanation of only one word or phrase.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find writing difficult may draw a spider diagram with labelled spokes in place of the list. Students from schools with non-standard staffing (e.g., a single-teacher school) should receive full credit for roles drawn from their real experience.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The written format directly mirrors the Textbook p. 13 reflection task and assesses the competency of explaining institutional roles through structured written output.

assessment_items.question_text: A student wrote this riddle: 'I have many shelves. People come to me to send letters and parcels. I help people stay in touch with those far away.' Which public place does this riddle describe?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is C. This item uses the chapter's riddle format to assess whether the student can read descriptive clues about a public institution and match them to the correct place. All four options appear in the chapter's community setting.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent the characteristics of a community place through a structured creative format and evaluate whether their representation communicates clearly.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has associated 'staying in touch' or 'helping people' with health services rather than reading the specific clue about letters and parcels — a confusion between service institutions in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has associated 'shelves' or 'official function' with a police station, missing the communication-and-delivery function described in the clues.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has associated 'many shelves' with a library or classroom and read the place as educational rather than communicative — a plausible but incorrect reading of the clue.

assessment_items.question_text: In Sikkim, the Khetala tradition brings together agricultural specialists at harvest time to help one another. The chapter has also shown Van Mahotsav, the Kanker bridge-building, the Magh Bihu feast, and the school team. What is the one big idea that connects all of these different examples? Explain in your own words and give one example from your own locality that shows the same idea.
look_for: Clear identification of a connecting idea — e.g., 'people with different skills working together for a shared goal', 'community cooperation across different places and traditions', or an equivalent formulation in the student's own words.
At least two of the chapter's examples used as evidence for the connecting idea (not just listed, but briefly explained).
A genuine example from the student's own locality or family experience that reflects the same connecting idea.

A response that goes beyond 'helping is good' to articulate what specifically makes these examples alike — the structure of cooperation, the diversity of contributors, the shared benefit, or the cultural embeddedness of the practice.
Coherence: the local example must logically connect to the identified big idea, not merely be a different example of community activity.
assessment_items.annotation: This is a synthesis item. The student's local example will vary by region — mark on the quality of the connection made, not on which example is chosen. A student who names the big idea precisely but offers a weak local example scores lower than one whose idea statement is less polished but whose local example is genuinely well-connected. Regional variation in the local example is expected and acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect community roles, shared spaces, cultural practices, and cooperative action into a coherent understanding of how people live and work together.
